'''Mitchel Resnick''' (born June 12, 1956) is an American computer scientist. He is the [[LEGO]] Papert Professor of Learning Research at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) [[MIT Media Lab|Media Lab]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.media.mit.edu/people/mres |title=Mitchel Resnick: Lifelong Kindergarten |website=[[MIT Media Lab]] |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |access-date=2019-08-03}}</ref> and is the founder of [[Scratch (programming language)|Scratch]]. {{As of|2019}}, Resnick serves as head of the Media Arts and Sciences academic program, which grants [[master's degree]]s and [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.s]] at the MIT Media Lab.

Resnick's research group has developed a variety of educational tools that engage people in new types of design activities and learning experiences, including the ''Programmable Bricks'' that were the basis for the [[Lego Mindstorms]] and [[StarLogo]] software. He cofounded the [[Computer Clubhouse]], a network of learning centers for youth from under-served communities. Resnick is also a cofounder and a co-principal investigator of the [[Center for Civic Media]] at MIT.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://civic.mit.edu/ |title=MIT Center for Civic Media |author=<!--Unstated--> |website=MIT Center for Civic Media }}</ref> Resnick is also involved in the next generation of Programmable Bricks, and the [[One Laptop per Child]] project which designed the [[OLPC XO]] ($100 laptop).

==Education==
Resnick, a graduate of [[Haverford High School]], earned a B.A. in physics at [[Princeton University]] (1978), and [[Master of Science|M.S.]] and Ph.D. degrees in [[computer science]] at MIT (1988, 1992).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Person Overview ‹ Mitchel Resnick |url=https://www.media.mit.edu/people/mres/overview/ |access-date=2023-10-10 |website=MIT Media Lab}}</ref>

==Career==
He worked for five years as a science–technology journalist for [[Business Week]] magazine, and he has consulted widely on the uses of computers in education. Resnick was awarded a [[National Science Foundation]] Young Investigator Award in 1993.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=9358519 |title=NSF Young Investigator Award |author=<!--Unstated--> |website=National Science Foundation |access-date=2019-08-03}}</ref> He has collaborated extensively with researchers such as [[Natalie Rusk]], [[Brian Silverman]], and [[Yasmin Kafai]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mitchel Resnick Publications |url=https://web.media.mit.edu/~mres/papers.html |website=MIT Media Lab |access-date=2015-10-28}}</ref>

==Awards==
Resnick is a winner of the 2011 [[Harold W. McGraw Prize in Education|Harold W. McGraw, Jr. Prize in Education]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.mheducation.com/ |title=Harold W. McGraw, Jr. Prize in Education, Winners |website=McGraw-Hill Education |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120703065942/http://www.mcgraw-hill.com/site/about-us/mcgraw-prize/winners |archive-date=2012-07-03 |access-date=2019-08-03}}</ref> He has been listed as one of the 100 most creative people in Business 2011 by Fast Company.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fastcompany.com/most-creative-people/2011/mitch-resnick-mit-media-lab |title=The 100 most creative people in business, 2011 |website=Fast Company |publisher=Mansueto Ventures |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111218111338/http://www.fastcompany.com/most-creative-people/2011/mitch-resnick-mit-media-lab |archive-date=2011-12-18 |access-date=2019-08-03}}</ref> In 2025, he was awarded the [[SIGCSE Award for Outstanding Contribution to Computer Science Education]].
